problem: Social robot navigation learning needs large, good-quality training data, but RL needs costly real-world trial and error or imperfect social simulators, and IL needs expensive teleoperated robot demonstrations (e.g., SCAND). Existing egocentric human video datasets such as Ego4D lack robot sensors like LiDAR, depth and odometry.
motivation: Humans are naturally skilled at socially compliant navigation and are plentiful, so recording them walking with robot-like sensors gives cheap, scalable, natural demonstrations. A wearable, replicable sensor suite could let groups worldwide collect diverse data, including cultural variation.
key_idea: Have humans wear a helmet-mounted multi-modal robotic sensor suite (3D LiDAR, stereo/depth camera, IMU, microphone array, 360° camera) while walking in public spaces, to build a large open dataset (MuSoHu) of socially compliant navigation demonstrations for robot learning.
insight: Human walking data with robot-style sensors can transfer to robots: behavior cloning on only ten MuSoHu trials produced a LiDAR-to-velocity policy that showed collision avoidance on a wheeled Ackermann robot and a quadruped. The paper also identifies embodiment mismatch (legged gait vs wheels), viewpoint mismatch (LiDAR height) and gait-induced IMU oscillation as the main challenges. This is qualitative proof-of-concept only, with no quantitative ablation.
method: Sensor suite: Helmet-mounted Velodyne VLP-16 3D LiDAR, ZED 2 stereo/depth camera with IMU (120° FOV), ReSpeaker Mic Array v2.0, Kodak Pixpro Orbit360 4K camera, wired to a laptop carried by the demonstrator; hardware and software open-sourced.

Data collection: Demonstrators walk to predefined goals in indoor and outdoor public spaces (GMU campus, Washington DC area), recorded via ROS bags; 360° video is saved to an SD card and synchronized with a clapboard.
Navigation contexts: Many trajectories are recorded three times under casual, neutral and rush contexts, which vary walking speed and safety distance.
Action/odometry extraction: Visual-inertial odometry from ZED 2 gives paths; linear and angular velocities are derived from consecutive odometry frames and smoothed with a Savitzky-Golay filter.
Annotations: 17 textual social-interaction tags per trajectory (e.g., Against Traffic 210, Sidewalk 160, Passing Conversational Groups 94), five of them new beyond SCAND, plus day/night tags.
Proof-of-concept BC: A behavior cloning policy maps raw LiDAR to linear and angular velocity, trained on ten trials and deployed on an AgileX Hunter SE and a Unitree Go1.

setting.backbone: Behavior cloning policy (raw LiDAR to linear/angular velocity) for the proof-of-concept; the main contribution is a dataset
setting.training_data: MuSoHu subset of ten navigation trials (full dataset ~20 h, ~100 km, 300 trials, 13 humans)
setting.observation: Egocentric human-worn multi-modal data: 3D LiDAR, stereo RGB + depth, IMU, microphone array, 360° video, visual-inertial odometry
setting.action_space: Continuous linear and angular velocity derived from odometry

numbers_note: No quantitative results; the proof-of-concept BC is shown only qualitatively (Fig. 4).
results: The paper presents MuSoHu, ~20 hours, ~100 km, 300 trajectories from 13 demonstrators in indoor and outdoor public spaces, with 17 interaction tags and context labels. A BC policy trained on ten trials shows learned obstacle avoidance on a Hunter SE and a Unitree Go1, with no quantitative comparison to baselines.
limitations: Embodiment and viewpoint mismatch: legged human gait, higher LiDAR mounting and vertical IMU oscillation differ from robot data, so transfer learning or mismatched-observation imitation is needed.
Validation is only a small qualitative BC demo (ten trials) with no quantitative metrics or baselines.
The 360° camera cannot be streamed to ROS and needs manual clapboard synchronization; actions are inferred from odometry rather than recorded.
